outcome: Since 26 January 2024 one event bears on the problem: King and Williams (online 31 August 2026) prove that N(t) is bounded for integers t with proportionately large prime-power factors, a restricted class of t. The conjecture itself is still open on every source read, the main partial progress is the 2021 interior result of Matomäki, Radziwiłł, Shao, Tao and Teräväinen (before the window), and no AI system was found connected to the problem.
problem_asks: (1) A single absolute constant M such that for every integer t >= 2 the number N(t) of positions (n, m) in Pascal's triangle with C(n, m) = t is at most M, i.e. N(t) = O(1). (2) The bound must be uniform over all entries other than 1 (every t >= 2); the entry 1 is excluded because it appears infinitely often. (3) The statement asks only whether such a finite bound exists, not for its value. Convention to note: the literature counts solutions of C(n, m) = t with 1 <= m < n, and the Wikipedia statement speaks of 'multiplicities', so mirror positions (m and n - m) are both counted in the examples (e.g. 3003 has eight positions, including (3003, 1) and (3003, 3002)).

events.what_happened: Matomäki, Radziwiłł, Shao, Tao and Teräväinen post 'Singmaster's conjecture in the interior of Pascal's triangle' to arXiv (2106.03335) on 7 June 2021; Tao announces it on his blog the same day. Theorem 1, as paraphrased in Tao's post: for fixed 0 < ε < 1 and t sufficiently large depending on ε, C(n, m) = t has at most two solutions with exp(log^{2/3+ε} n) <= m <= n/2, hence at most four in the symmetric interior exp(log^{2/3+ε} n) <= m <= n - exp(log^{2/3+ε} n); and at most one solution in the narrower range up to n/exp(log^{1-ε} n). The abstract also gives analogous results for falling factorials. Journal version: Quart. J. Math. 73 (2022) 1137-1177, DOI 10.1093/qmath/haac006.
events.revisions: arXiv abstract page as fetched lists only v1 (Mon 7 Jun 2021). Journal publication 2022 (Quart. J. Math. 73 (2022)).
events.delivers: Settles the bound for the interior of the triangle only: for each ε, once t is at least a threshold depending on ε, at most four solutions with m in the interior range and at most two in each half. The 'at most two' per half is sharp by an infinite Fibonacci family. Restrictions: interior only; t sufficiently large depending on ε, so the theorem as stated gives no bound for small t; no uniform constant over all t >= 2.
events.remains: Part (1) and part (2) of problem_asks for all t >= 2. In particular the boundary region 2 <= m < exp(log^{2/3+ε} n), i.e. the edges of the triangle, and every t below the threshold depending on ε. Tao's post says verifying the full conjecture reduces to the boundary region, which this paper does not treat.

events.what_happened: Zachary King and R. Scott Williams (Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Central Oklahoma), 'A bound for repeated binomial coefficients having large prime power factors', Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics 32(2) (2026) 430-438, DOI 10.7546/nntdm.2026.32.2.430-438. Abstract as read on the journal page: they bound N(t), the number of ways of writing t as a binomial coefficient, using properties of Pascal's triangle under modular arithmetic; they show N(t) is bounded for t with proportionately 'large' prime power factors; they say stronger bounds may be possible by this method. Keywords include Singmaster's Conjecture. No arXiv preprint was found.
events.revisions: Online First 31 August 2026, accepted 27 August 2026 (journal page). Received October 2025 and revised 13 July 2026 appear in a search-result snippet of the PDF, which I could not read directly.
events.delivers: N(t) is bounded for integers t whose prime-power factors are 'proportionately large' (the exact condition and constant are in the PDF, which I could not read). A search-result snippet, not verified in the full text, gives a corollary: for fixed r, if t > 1 is sufficiently large, pq is a prime-power factor of t, and t^(1/r) <= pq, then N(t) <= 2r. Restriction: only t with a large prime-power factor; no bound for general t and no uniform constant over all t >= 2.
events.remains: Parts (1) and (2) of problem_asks for every t >= 2 that does not have the required prime-power structure. The abstract says stronger bounds 'may be possible' but gives none.

events.what_happened: Daniel Kane, 'Improved bounds on the number of ways of expressing t as a binomial coefficient', Integers 7 (2007) A53. Improves the Abbott-Erdős-Hanson bound to N(t) = O((log t)(log log log t)/(log log t)^3). Kane's UCSD page carries two papers: the first gives the (log log t)^2 version and the second, dated 27 February 2007 in a search snippet, gives the cubic version.
events.revisions: Two Kane files on his UCSD page (combinations.pdf and combinations2.pdf). The date 27 February 2007 for the second is from a search snippet; the PDF was not readable by the fetch tool.
events.delivers: Unconditional bound N(t) = O((log t)(log log log t)/(log log t)^3) for all t > 1. This grows with t, so it is not boundedness and does not answer part (1).
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no uniform constant M is given.

events.what_happened: H. L. Abbott, P. Erdős and D. Hanson, 'On the number of times an integer occurs as a binomial coefficient', American Mathematical Monthly 81 (1974) 256-261. Improves Singmaster's O(log a) to O(log a / log log a); shows the average and normal order of N(t) is 2; shows that the number of t <= x with N(t) > 2 is O(sqrt x). Conditional on Cramér's conjecture on prime gaps, Wikipedia records N(a) = O((log a)^{2/3+ε}) for every ε > 0; one search summary of Kane's paper gives (log t)^{2/3} with no ε. I did not reconcile these.
events.delivers: Unconditional bound N(t) = O(log t / log log t); average order 2; exceptional count O(sqrt x). Conditional bound (under Cramér's conjecture) as above. None of this is boundedness.

events.what_happened: David Singmaster, 'Repeated binomial coefficients and Fibonacci numbers', Fibonacci Quarterly 13(4) (1975). Per search-result snippets (PDF not read): an infinite family of integers occurring at least six times, and a computer search up to 2^48 for further repetitions, reporting seven nontrivial repetitions in that range. The original 1971 note, 'How often does an integer occur as a binomial coefficient?' (Amer. Math. Monthly 78 (1971) 385-386), gave N(a) = O(log a) and posed the conjecture; it is not recorded as a separate event because it poses the problem rather than moving it.
events.delivers: A finite census up to 2^48 and an infinite family with at least six occurrences. A finite census of instances of a universal claim moves nothing; the family shows multiplicity 6 is attained infinitely often, which is compatible with boundedness.
events.directly_checkable: The census values and the Fibonacci family can be checked by hand from the stated formulas; not checked in this run.
events.object: The infinite family of integers occurring at least six times, given through Fibonacci-number formulas (as reported in the Open Problem Garden and Wikipedia summaries). Explicit.

disputes.summary: The Erdős problems database (problem 849) and its Lean formalisation in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/849.lean) state the problem as: for every t >= 1 there is an integer a such that C(n, k) = a with 1 <= k <= n/2 has exactly t solutions. That asks whether every multiplicity is attained. Wikipedia and the Singmaster literature state it as a bound on multiplicities. The database says both Erdős and Singmaster believed the answer is 'no' and that there is an absolute upper bound, so it links the two. These are different questions; the Lean statement uses the existence form with answer(sorry) and proof sorry, and it uses Set.ncard, which returns 0 for infinite sets.

The conditional bound of Abbott, Erdős and Hanson under Cramér's conjecture is written as (log a)^{2/3+ε} in Wikipedia but as (log t)^{2/3} in one search summary of Kane's paper. Not reconciled; the exponent should be checked against the 1974 paper.

summary: Found: one in-window event and a set of earlier results. The in-window event is King and Williams (NNTDM 32(2), 2026, online 31 August 2026), which shows N(t) is bounded for integers with proportionately large prime-power factors. I read only the journal abstract page; the PDF returned binary, so the theorem's exact class and constant are not verified, and the corollary (N(t) <= 2r when t^(1/r) <= pq) comes from a search snippet. The result is a bound on the named quantity for a subclass of t, so it is a partial result by scope, not a resolution, and nothing public has engaged with it yet. The earlier partial result is Matomäki, Radziwiłł, Shao, Tao and Teräväinen (arXiv 7 June 2021; QJM 2022), which settles the bound in the interior of the triangle for t sufficiently large depending on ε. Its boundary region, the edges of the triangle, is open, and Tao's post says the full conjecture reduces to it. Unconditional bounds remain Kane's (2007) and Abbott, Erdős and Hanson's (1974), both growing with t. The Wikipedia article I read (current version, not the 26 January 2024 revision) and Open Problem Garden both still give 3003 as the only known eight-fold value and say it is not known whether any value occurs more than eight times; the NNTDM paper's search snippet repeats that. The Erdős database and its Lean file treat the problem as the existence question for every multiplicity t, which I record as a scope variant rather than the same problem; its history page shows no status change after the 2025-10-20 snapshot, and its forum thread has no posts. Close calls: (a) King and Williams: as a bound on N(t), it moves a quantity the problem names, which is the kind of result section 2.1 keeps; as a uniform bound it covers only a subclass of t, and the 'large prime-power factor' condition excludes most t. Both readings are recorded. (b) MRSTT: the database and some search summaries describe it as 'settling' the interior, while the arXiv abstract and Tao's post say it is interior-only and conditional on t being large; I read it as partial. AI: no AI system was found connected to Singmaster's conjecture across roughly 44 searches. Searches for AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude with this problem returned nothing relevant, and the Erdős database's AI-assisted resolutions that surfaced (problems 728, 848, 1026 and others) are different problems. One open lead: AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv 2605.22763, which states it resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems) does not list its problems in the text I read, so whether 849 is among them is unknown. Sra's 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (arXiv 2608.29595) names GPT Pro, but its abstract page does not mention Singmaster or binomial coefficients; I did not read its full text. The gcd paper (arXiv 2606.22997, June 2026) credits an AI agent, but it concerns gcds, not repetitions, so I record it as a discounted event. Disclosed cost: none found.
competing_reading: For King and Williams: a reader who weighs §2.1 strictly can say the paper advances the named quantity N(t) and is therefore the in-window event that should count, since the problem's status is about bounded multiplicities and the paper proves boundedness for a class. The opposing reading is that a bound valid only for t with large prime-power factors leaves the universal claim open, so it should be recorded as partial progress, not a resolution. For MRSTT: a reader could take 'at most four solutions in the interior, for t large' as the conjecture for most of the triangle, which is how some summaries phrase it; the stronger reading is that the edges and small t are open, so the conjecture is open. For the Erdős 849 version: the database treats its existence question and Singmaster's bound as one problem, so a reader using the database's statement would reach different event sets and a different verdict than one using Wikipedia's wording.
what_would_settle_it: (1) For King and Williams: the full PDF, to read the exact theorem (the class of t and the constant), any acknowledgements (to settle AI involvement), and whether the corollary in the snippet matches it. (2) For AI involvement on Erdős 849: the list of the nine Erdős problems AlphaProof Nexus resolved (arXiv 2605.22763) and whether 849 is among them, plus any statement in that paper about binomial coefficients. (3) For the boundary: any later paper treating 2 <= m < exp(log^{2/3+ε} n) or the small-t cases. (4) For the uniform question: any proof of N(t) = O(1) for all t >= 2, or a family of t with unbounded N(t), either of which would change the picture completely. (5) For the wording: the 26 January 2024 Wikipedia revision and its citations, to confirm which version of the problem the frozen list uses.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether N(t) is uniformly bounded for all t >= 2. King and Williams (online 31 August 2026, after the snapshot) prove boundedness for a restricted class of t (those with proportionately large prime-power factors): a restriction of the question, so case; it was accepted by a refereed journal of record (NNTDM), which meets the digestion bar, and nothing in the record gives a specific reason to doubt it. MRSTT 2021 settles the interior region for large t: case, refereed in QJM, before the snapshot. Kane and Abbott-Erdős-Hanson give growing bounds on N(t), so bound. Singmaster's 1975 census and de Weger's six-fold value are finite instances; the six-fold family is compatible with boundedness and neither witnesses nor contradicts the statement. Jenkins (a different equation), de Koninck et al. (multinomial), Bazsó et al. (Stirling numbers) and the gcd criterion (gcds, not multiplicities) are variants. The gcd paper credits an AI agent, but the record leaves its systems list empty and the result is not about this problem, so its AI role is none. No AI role was found in any event that bears on the problem.
judgement.doubts: King and Williams: the full text was not read, so the exact class of t and the corollary N(t) <= 2r rest on the abstract and a search snippet. The paper has had no outside engagement in six weeks, and I count it as digested only because a refereed journal accepted it. The record left open whether Erdős 849 is among the AlphaProof Nexus resolutions, but that database states a different (existence) form of the problem.
